content.text:
The child who bursts into tears at the doctor's

Just mentioning a trip to the doctor makes your child's tail droop, and in the waiting room, another child's crying sets their heart pounding. Watching a child pour out tears in front of a shot hurts a parent's heart too.

It's only natural for a child to be afraid of shots. An unfamiliar place, the worry that it might hurt, and the feeling of not being in control all pile up. Rather than making them suppress this fear, teaching them how to understand and manage it helps a child find courage, little by little.

Curious about the story of the child afraid of shots? We look at the lessons of this story alongside the pictures. Meet the key scenes of the story, too. Read the story of the child afraid of shots with your child and talk it over together. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "A Poke of the Shot, Poof Go the Germs!" — fear-of-the-doctor storybooks, vaccination storybooks, emotion-regulation storybooks, and more.
content.caption: Being afraid of shots is a perfectly natural feeling.

content.alt: 15. A Poke of the Shot, Poof Go the Germs! - Why the power to manage fear matters
content.text:
Why the power to manage fear matters

The experience of getting through the fear of a shot becomes a great strength for the other scary moments a child will meet in the future. Being scared, yet understanding why and practicing steadying your own heart, plants the seed of the ability to regulate emotions.

What matters isn't a false reassurance like "it won't hurt," but knowing why it's needed and having a small action you can do yourself. When a child has their own method — take a deep breath and hold out their arm — they feel a sense of control even in the face of fear.
content.caption: A small action you can do yourself builds courage.

content.alt: 15. A Poke of the Shot, Poof Go the Germs! - Hori's story of the soldiers inside the body
content.text:
Hori's story of the soldiers inside the body

In "A Poke of the Shot, Poof Go the Germs!", Hori too is scared of the shot, his heart pounding in the waiting room. Just then, a kind elephant doctor tells him a story: "Inside your body live brave little soldiers."

Imagining that the shot helps the soldiers who have grown weak against the germs, Hori chants, "Breathe out, hooo — hold out your arm — and think of the brave soldiers!" Poke! But it didn't hurt at all, more than he expected. The soldiers inside rush in, the germs go poof and vanish, and Hori didn't cry.
content.caption: Imagining the shot as help for the soldiers inside my body.

content.alt: 15. A Poke of the Shot, Poof Go the Germs! - Let's practice together at home
content.text:
Let's practice together at home

After reading the book, connect the story to a real doctor's visit. First, instead of a false "it won't hurt," explain why the shot is needed at your child's level. Understanding it reduces the fear.

Second, practice taking a deep breath and holding out an arm ahead of time, so your child has a method they can do on their own. Third, when they endure or overcome the fear, praise them specifically — "You were so brave!" — so they feel proud of themselves.
content.caption: Praise the moment they overcame it, specifically.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I reassure a child who is afraid of shots?

A. Don't frighten them; tell them the shot is a dependable helper that fights off germs. Letting them know in advance that it's over quickly after one little poke helps reduce the fear.

Q. What should I prepare before a vaccination?

A. Picturing the situation with a story ahead of time lets your child prepare their heart. Even a child afraid of shots finds courage when they hear a story about a shot going poke and the germs going poof.

Q. How do I encourage them after the shot?

A. Praise them warmly for enduring it well, give them a hug, and acknowledge their courage. Empathizing with how much it hurt helps them face the next visit a little more bravely.
